THE EGG& THE LEDGER
Reading a state budget.
A 45 minute session.
OPEN WITH THIS

What is our
understanding
of a budget?

Simplest version: A State Budget Document is a government document that shows how public money is planned to be spent during a financial year.

OPEN ON YOUTUBE ↗

If the player above shows an error, opening this file from disk (rather than a website) blocks YouTube's embed check — use the “Open on YouTube” link in the corner instead. Write the creator's name on this slide before you present.

A statement of the money a government expects to receive and expects to spend between 1 April and 31 March, placed before the legislature and passed as an Appropriation Act.

It is an estimate. Nothing in it has happened yet.

It is permission, not money. Without the Appropriation Act no rupee leaves the Consolidated Fund.

It is the accountability document between the executive, the legislature and the public.

For the Union this is called the Annual Financial Statement, under Article 112. For states it is Article 202, and it is the same thing. Article 266 creates the Consolidated Fund.
START HERE

One egg.
One ledger.

On a Tuesday morning Meera boils 34 eggs at the anganwadi centre in her village. One egg for every child who turns up.

Somebody paid for those eggs. Somebody wrote the number down a year earlier. Somebody will check, two years later, whether the money went where it was promised.

That whole chain is the budget. We are going to walk it backwards.

Meera is an illustration, not a case study. The accounting around her is real.

THE WORDS, EXPLAINED

Two questions,
four boxes

The same two questions as before give you four categories. Read this slide once, then use it as a reference on the next one.

Money flowWhat it meansRevenueCapital
Coming inReceiptRevenue ReceiptCapital Receipt
Going outExpenditureRevenue ExpenditureCapital Expenditure

Revenue Receipt

Money the government receives that does not create a debt and does not reduce anything it owns. It mostly funds day to day running.

GST and state taxes, stamp duty, excise duty, fees collected by departments, fines and penalties, interest the government receives, grants in aid from the Centre.

Capital Receipt

Money coming in that either creates a debt or reduces an asset the government owns.

Creates a debt: a market loan, government bonds, loans from financial institutions, a Ways and Means Advance.

Reduces an asset: recovering a loan the government had given out, or the proceeds from selling government equity.

Revenue Expenditure

Spending on the normal running of government. It does not create a physical or financial asset.

Salaries, electricity bills, rent, routine maintenance, medicines used by patients, training, travel, office expenses, interest paid on government debt, most grants in aid.

Capital Expenditure

Spending that creates, buys or improves an asset, or that pays down a debt. It changes what the government owns or owes.

Building a school, building a hospital, buying major machinery, building roads, acquiring land, investing in a public sector undertaking, loans the government gives out.

THE WORDS, IN PRACTICE

Two questions,
four boxes

Same four boxes. New examples, none repeated from the last slide. Drag each one in.

Revenue

Happens every year. Leaves nothing behind.

Capital

Happens once. Leaves an asset or a debt behind.

Guessing wrong and reading why is worth more than guessing right.

FOLLOW IT YOURSELF

Follow
the money

Seven ordinary things. Pick one and watch it climb into the ledger.

The major head, the four digit code at the end of each chain, is fixed nationally. What the scheme is called below that level changes from state to state. Check the sub-head names in your own state's Detailed Demands for Grants.
WHY ANY OF THIS MATTERS

Where policy
meets money

A policy says what the government wants to do. A budget shows the resources provided for that priority. The real question is what gets authorised, spent and delivered.

It makes priorities visible

A policy commitment becomes easier to track when it has a budget head, code and amount attached to it.

It sets a financial boundary

A department can spend public money only within the authority and limits provided through the budget and appropriation process.

It creates a money trail

We can follow public money from budget provision to authorisation, release and expenditure, and ask what happened to it.

Meera's eggs began with a policy commitment: improve child nutrition.

The government then provided resources for the nutrition programme through the budget. The legislature authorised the expenditure, funds were released, and the programme procured and distributed the food.

But the budget number alone does not put an egg in Meera's hand.

We have to follow the money, from provision → authorisation → expenditure → delivery.
THE WORDS, 3 OF 4

Three pots
of money

Consolidated Fund

The main account. Everything the state earns or borrows goes in here, and nothing leaves without a vote. Meera's eggs were paid from this pot. Nearly all your reading happens here.

Contingency Fund

A small emergency float. The government can spend from it first and get approval afterwards. You will rarely need to read it.

Public Account

Money the government holds for other people, like provident fund deposits and small savings. It is a caretaker here, not an owner, so no vote is needed.

The test is ownership. If the money belongs to the government, it sits in the Consolidated Fund and the legislature has to approve spending it. If the government is only holding it for someone else, it sits in the Public Account.

The three pots, drawn out in full

Every rupee in the accounts sits somewhere on this chart. Find the Consolidated Fund first, then follow it down: money comes in on the left, goes out on the right.

Redrawn for this deck. Structure follows Chart 1.4, Structure of Government Accounts, in the CAG State Finances Audit Report, Uttar Pradesh (Report No. 6), p. 7.

WHAT AM I LOOKING AT?

The budget
has an address

A budget number is an address. It tells you where the spending sits, what it is for, what kind of spending it is, and how much is provided. Nine components make up that address.

ComponentWhat are you askingStandard
Grant / DemandWhose expenditure is thisState specific
Revenue / CapitalWhat broad type of spendingCommon
Major HeadWhat broad functionCommon
Sub-Major HeadWhich area of that functionCommon
Minor HeadWhich specific functional areaCommon
Sub-HeadWhich scheme or categoryCan vary
Detailed HeadWhich component or activityCan vary
Object HeadWhat kind of expenditureCommon framework, local codes
Actuals, BE, REHow much, and when

means the idea works the same in every government. means the label or the code is set locally, so it is worth checking each time.

1 · Grant / Demand — Grant No. 049, Dept. of Women & Child Welfare
2 · Revenue / Capital — this line sits under Revenue
3 · Major Head — 2235, Social Security and Welfare
4 · Sub-Major Head — 02, Social Welfare
5 · Minor Head — 102, Child Welfare
6 · Sub-Head — 01, Centrally Sponsored Schemes
7 · Detailed Head — 0106, Child Welfare Committee
8 · Object Head — 07, Honorarium
9 · Actuals, BE, RE — ₹975.04 / 2399.94 / 2399.94 / 2471.93 lakh
Three documents behind this deck: the UP grant-wise detailed estimates for Women and Child Welfare, 2026-27; the CGA List of Major and Minor Heads for the classification that is common everywhere; and Maharashtra's BEAMS, referenced by name later on this slide set to show that a real live budget system exposes these same layers for browsing.
WHOSE MONEY?

First, find
the grant

A Grant, or Demand for Grant, is the bundle of spending that gets presented to the legislature for a vote. It is not the same thing as the accounting Major Head. A grant is a legislative unit. A major head is an accounting unit. The two sit side by side on the same page but answer different questions.

UP WCD Budget 2026-27, grant identification

Grant No. 049, Uttar Pradesh, Department of Women and Child Welfare. The legislative unit is a plain number, and Major Head 2235 sits right inside the same detailed estimate.

Maharashtra Gender Budget Statement 2025-26, page 33

Demand X-01, Maharashtra, Women and Child Development Department. Here the legislative unit is coded X-01, not a number at all — but the scheme underneath still carries Major Head 2235, the same head UP uses.

The important point. Grant numbers are not universal. 049 is Women and Child Welfare in this UP budget only because UP assigned it that number. A different state, or a different year, can hand 049 to an entirely different department.

Wrong: 049 always means Women and Child Welfare.
Right: 049 is WCD's grant number in the UP 2026-27 budget.
WHAT KIND OF MONEY?

Then: revenue
or capital?

Revenue is the regular, current spending that keeps a service running. Capital is spending that creates, buys or improves an asset. Every major head sits on one side of that line, and the same subject usually has a matching head on each side. Grant 049 prints both, one above the other, on the same page.

SubjectRevenueCapital
Nutrition22364236
General Education22024202
Technical Education22034202
Sports and Youth Services22044202
Medical and Public Health22104210
Family Welfare22114211
Social Security and Welfare22354235
UP WCD Budget 2026-27, page 3 — revenue side

What is revenue. Head 2235, Social Security and Welfare. Salaries, honorarium for anganwadi workers, diet expenses, the food itself. The money goes out and nothing is left standing afterwards. BE 2026-27: Rs 14,95,740.16 lakh.

UP WCD Budget 2026-27, page 3 — capital side

What is capital. Head 4235, the same subject with a 4 in front. Building anganwadi centres, constructing shelter homes and hostels, buying vehicles. BE 2026-27: Rs 70,523.00 lakh.

Read the ratio, not just the pair. Revenue is about twenty-one times capital in this grant. That is normal for a welfare department that mostly pays people and buys food, rather than one that mostly builds. It also means a headline cut to "the WCD budget" almost always lands on the revenue side, which is where the eggs are.
The Controller General of Accounts classification separates Revenue Receipt Heads, Revenue Expenditure Heads and Capital Account Expenditure Heads by design, and lists these as worked examples: 2202 General Education, 2203 Technical Education, 2204 Sports and Youth Services, 2210 Medical and Public Health, 2211 Family Welfare, 2235 Social Security and Welfare on the revenue side, with 4202, 4210, 4211 and 4235 as their capital twins, plus 4236 for Nutrition. Source: CGA, List of Major and Minor Heads of Account of Union and States. Figures as printed in the UP WCD detailed estimates, Grant No. 049, page 3.

Tiers one to four are printed as a single running header, which is why one screenshot carries three of them. The document never spells out the word "Sub-Major" or "Minor Head" — it just prints the numbers in order and expects you to know the order. That is the whole skill.
This is the same egg from the start of the session, now with its full address. The anganwadi centre and the primary school are both cooking under the same nutrition logic, but they sit under different departments, different major heads and different grants. That is why the address matters more than the name of the scheme.
Maharashtra shows a different shape at this level: a scheme code such as 22351316 for Mahila Aarthik Vikas Mahamandal does not map onto the same six boxes the way this UP example does. No Maharashtra document was supplied for this session, so this point is stated without a screenshot. The conceptual message still holds: the accounting classification is common everywhere. The scheme or programme layer on top of it is not. Source for the common layer: CGA, List of Major and Minor Heads of Account of Union and States, issued by the Ministry of Finance, Department of Expenditure.
HOW MUCH, AND WHEN?

The financial
year columns

Now that you know where the money sits, the last question is how much and for which year. Every grant prints the same four columns, in the same order, always — at the top of the grant and again beside every single scheme line.

ColumnMeaning
ActualsWhat was really spent, audited, two years behind
BEBudget Estimate, the original provision for that year
RERevised Estimate, the mid-year correction
BEBudget Estimate for the year about to start
UP WCD Budget 2026-27, page 3. Grant 049, revenue account, Rs lakh.
2024-25 Act.2025-26 BE2025-26 RE2026-27 BE
8,74,935.7913,52,569.5913,26,792.4214,95,740.16

At the top of the grant. The 2025-26 provision was trimmed slightly at revision, from 13,52,569.59 to 13,26,792.42. The new BE then rises about 12.7 per cent above that revised figure.

UP WCD Budget 2026-27, page 8. Head 0125, object head 43, Rs lakh.
2024-25 Act.2025-26 BE2025-26 RE2026-27 BE
1,20,790.354,11,860.004,11,860.003,84,425.97

One scheme line down. Same four columns, same order. BE and RE for 2025-26 are identical here, so nothing was corrected mid-year. The new BE is about 6.7 per cent lower than both.

Comparing BE to BE across years is the trap from earlier in this session. Compare BE 2026-27 to RE 2025-26, not to BE 2025-26. On the grant total that turns a 10.6 per cent rise into a 12.7 per cent rise; on the anganwadi line it makes no difference at all, because BE and RE were the same.
One more trap in the Actuals column. The 2024-25 actual against head 0125 reads 1,20,790.35 lakh, which looks like a collapse next to a 4,11,860.00 provision. It is not. A second 1,16,855.52 lakh for the same anganwadi Poshan state share is parked on page 14 under code 8925, in a block labelled Lump Sum for Centrally Sponsored Schemes, 2024-25 Actuals only. Add the two and the real actual is about 2,37,645.87 lakh. Never read an Actuals figure without checking whether the same scheme also appears under a lump-sum code.
HOW THE NUMBER GOT THERE

Plan. Allocate.
Spend. Audit.

Click a stage. Notice that any single year is being planned, spent and audited at the same time, in three different rooms.

The budget you read in February was started the previous October.
Meera's eggs were decided in a Finance Department room in December, voted in March, cooked in August, and will be audited the year after next by someone who has never met her.
THE CAST

Five actors,
one money trail

Finance Dept

PLANS & COORDINATES

Prepares the budget framework, coordinates resource allocation and manages the government's overall financial position.

Line Dept

PLANS & DELIVERS

Identifies programme needs, prepares its budget demands and implements programmes within the funds authorised to it.

WCD → nutrition. Health → hospitals. Education → schools.

Legislature

AUTHORISES

Examines and votes on Demands for Grants and passes the Appropriation Act, providing legislative authority for expenditure.

CAG

AUDITS

Examines government accounts and whether public money was used in accordance with applicable rules and authorisation, and reports to the legislature.

Public Accounts Cttee

QUESTIONS

Examines CAG reports and questions the government on findings from the audit.

The Line Department is the one closest to “What are we actually trying to deliver?” It is where the budget line stops being a number and becomes a programme.
WHOSE MONEY IS IT

Three ways a scheme
gets paid for

The allocation number means nothing until you know which of these three you are looking at, because the state's exposure is completely different in each.

SHARED

Centrally Sponsored

The Centre and the state split the bill. The state has to find its share or the central money goes unclaimed. It flows through the state budget, so you will see it there.

PM POSHAN, Samagra Shiksha, National Health Mission, Poshan Abhiyaan and Saksham Anganwadi.

ALL CENTRE

Central Sector

Fully paid by the Centre with no state share. It may not appear in the state budget at all, which is a common cause of double counting.

PM-KISAN.

ALL STATE

State scheme

Paid for entirely by the state. Its own priority and its own risk. This is where you see real political preference.

Rythu Bharosa, Aasara pensions, Arogya Lakshmi, Kalyana Lakshmi, Mission Bhagiratha.

The usual split for a shared scheme is 60:40, with 90:10 for North Eastern and Himalayan states and some components paid fully by the Centre. Ratios are revised from time to time, so check the specific scheme and year rather than assuming. States also sometimes top up above the shared norm, which is a fourth pattern hiding inside the third.

Where to find it. Every state publishes this as a PDF, usually titled Detailed Estimates of Expenditure, Demand for Grants or Budget at a Glance — Volume II/III, on the state Finance Department's website, alongside the Finance Minister's speech and the Annual Financial Statement. Search “[your state] detailed estimates budget [year] pdf” if it is not obvious from the department homepage.

ComponentWhat you're askingTypeWrite in what you found
Grant / DemandWhose expenditure is this
Revenue / CapitalWhat broad type of spending
Major HeadWhat broad function
Sub-Major HeadWhich area of that function
Minor HeadWhich specific functional area
Sub-HeadWhich scheme or category
Detailed HeadWhich component or activity
Object HeadWhat kind of expenditure, in local codes
ActualsWhat was really spent, two years back
BE, this yearOriginal provision for the year now closing
RE, this yearThe mid-year correction to that provision
BE, next yearProvision for the year about to start

works the same in every state's document, because it follows the CGA classification. is set locally — your state may use different words, a different numbering scheme, or fold two tiers into one. Note the difference in the last column rather than forcing your document to match this deck's example.

Why this works

Filling in row three, Major Head, is the hard one and the whole point. Nobody hands you the code — you find it by matching the scheme name to a heading in the document. Do that once on your own state, and the UP examples earlier in this deck stop being the only budget you can read.

If you finish early

Check whether your scheme also appears under a lump-sum or restructured code elsewhere in the document, the way the anganwadi Poshan line did on slide 12. Then find that scheme's capital twin (swap the leading 2 for a 4, or 3 for a 4) and see whether anything at all is allocated there. A blank cell is a real answer.

Nine components, same order as slide 8. Grant numbers, sub-head, detailed head and object codes are set by each state, so treat every yellow-dot row as something to verify locally rather than assume. If your state's document skips a tier or merges two together, write down what it does instead — that gap is itself the finding.
